clinicalPearls: WPW syndrome is the combination of ventricular pre-excitation on the resting ECG and symptomatic tachyarrhythmia; pre-excitation without symptoms is termed a WPW pattern.
The classic triad is a short PR interval, a slurred delta wave and a widened QRS, reflecting fusion of accessory-pathway and nodal ventricular activation.
The delta-wave vector and precordial transition allow bedside prediction of pathway location, guiding ablation.
Orthodromic AVRT is the commonest tachycardia, but pre-excited atrial fibrillation is the most dangerous because it can conduct rapidly and degenerate to ventricular fibrillation.
An irregular, broad, rapid tachycardia with varying QRS morphology should raise immediate suspicion of pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
AV-nodal blocking drugs including adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem and digoxin are contraindicated in pre-excited atrial fibrillation as they can accelerate pathway conduction.
Abrupt, complete loss of pre-excitation during exercise or with procainamide suggests a pathway with a long refractory period and lower risk.
Ebstein anomaly is associated with WPW and frequently with multiple right-sided accessory pathways.
reference.pathophysiology: The syndrome results from a congenital accessory atrioventricular pathway that bypasses the physiological delay of the atrioventricular node, allowing early activation of ventricular myocardium (pre-excitation). Because the pathway conducts faster than the node, part of the ventricle depolarises early, shortening the PR interval and inscribing a delta wave, while the remainder is activated normally, producing a fusion QRS. The same pathway provides a limb for macroreentrant tachycardia. When atrial fibrillation develops, an accessory pathway with a short antegrade refractory period can transmit disorganised atrial impulses to the ventricle at extremely high rates, and this rapid irregular ventricular response may deteriorate into ventricular fibrillation and sudden death.
additionalDifferentials: concealed accessory pathway atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia
bundle branch block mimicking a wide QRS
additionalInvestigations: twelve-lead ECG to characterise the delta wave and localise the pathway
exercise stress testing to assess abrupt loss of pre-excitation
transthoracic echocardiography to exclude Ebstein anomaly and cardiomyopathy
electrophysiological study with measurement of the shortest pre-excited RR interval in atrial fibrillation
procainamide or other pharmacological challenge to gauge pathway refractoriness
redFlags: pre-excited atrial fibrillation with a very short shortest pre-excited RR interval
syncope, particularly during exertion or palpitations
resuscitated cardiac arrest or documented ventricular fibrillation
family history of sudden death with pre-excitation
haemodynamic instability during any wide-complex tachycardia
reference.prognosis: Most patients have an excellent prognosis and catheter ablation is curative with a high success rate, but a small subset with rapidly conducting pathways are at risk of sudden cardiac death, which may occasionally be the first manifestation. Risk stratification of asymptomatic pre-excitation is therefore central to management.
pitfalls: Treating pre-excited atrial fibrillation with AV-nodal blockers and precipitating ventricular fibrillation.
Dismissing asymptomatic pre-excitation without considering risk stratification in higher-risk occupations or athletes.
Confusing a fusion or pre-excited complex with myocardial infarction because of pseudo-Q waves and repolarisation change.
Assuming a single pathway when multiple pathways, especially in Ebstein anomaly, are present.
Interpreting intermittent pre-excitation as invariably low-risk without confirming it is abrupt and rate-related.
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC Guidelines for the management of patients with supraventricular tachycardia
Zipes Cardiac Electrophysiology: From Cell to Bedside
management: Radiofrequency catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is the curative mainstay for symptomatic pre-excitation and recurrent tachyarrhythmia
Acute orthodromic AVRT managed with vagal manoeuvres then adenosine or another short-acting AV-nodal blocker

Pre-excited atrial fibrillation treated with procainamide, flecainide or synchronised cardioversion while strictly avoiding adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem and digoxin, which can accelerate pathway conduction
Urgent synchronised electrical cardioversion for the haemodynamically unstable pre-excited patient
Risk stratification of asymptomatic pre-excitation by exercise testing and, in higher-risk occupations or findings, an electrophysiology study measuring the shortest pre-excited RR interval
Long-term suppressive antiarrhythmic therapy such as flecainide or propafenone where ablation is not undertaken
Cardiology and electrophysiology referral with transthoracic echocardiography to exclude Ebstein anomaly and cardiomyopathy
